# Results — Study 705 (Rounding Top / dome distribution) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim —
**a rounding top (dome distribution) marks distribution, and the confirmed
breakdown below the rim starts a sustained decline — short it** — tested with the
closest **mechanical** detector (a least-squares parabola with negative curvature, a
good fit, an interior peak, sufficient height, and a first close below the left-rim
support). For each confirmed breakdown we **short at the next day's open** (one
execution lag) and measure the forward 10 / 20 / 60-day SHORT return against the
**every-bar SHORT base rate** and a **date-shuffle placebo**. As-of **2026-06-30**
(the last complete calendar month). Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted OHLC — SPY + 29 long-listed US large-caps (public, no key) |
| Window | 2004-01-02 → 2026-06-30 (**22.5** years; 5,658 bars/name) |
| Names | **30** (SPY + 29 large-caps) |
| Panel fingerprint | `9da1b7ce7758` |
| Detector | trailing window `base_len=90`; parabola $a<0$, $R^2\ge0.55$; vertex in central 60%; height $\ge0.08$ (log) above support; first close below the left-rim low; 30-bar cooldown |
| Timing / costs | short **t+1 open**, cover close at t+1+H (one lag); 5 bps one-way × NAV round trip **+ 30 bps/yr borrow** pro-rated over the holding horizon (short-only) |

> **Survivorship (named on the Signal axis — and, unlike Study 416, working
> *against* the pattern).** The basket is 30 names *still trading* in 2026. A
> surviving-names panel **cannot include names that were delisted, went bankrupt, or
> were taken private at a discount** after a confirmed rounding-top breakdown — the
> exact tail outcomes that would make the bearish claim look *best*. So this panel's
> null is, if anything, **conservative against the bullish direction and generous to
> nothing in particular for the bearish claim** — a confirmed-breakdown edge would
> have to show up in the survivors alone, and it doesn't. Chart figures are also
> **partly subjective**: we test one reasonable mechanical definition and report
> robustness to its knobs (below).

## The signal — confirmed breakdown (short) vs the every-bar SHORT base rate

The decisive test is **not** the breakdown short return against zero (which mixes in
the equity drift premium working *against* every short) but against the **base
rate** — the average forward SHORT return of a *random day* in the same names. The
placebo *p* is the share of 5,000 random-date draws (matched to the per-name
breakdown count, shorted the same way) whose pooled forward SHORT return **beats**
the observed breakdown mean.

| horizon | n breakdowns | gross (short) | net (5bps+borrow) | base rate (short) | win% | base win% | one-sample *t* vs 0 | HAC *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10-day | 227 | −0.76% | −0.88% | −0.59% | 46% | 43% | −1.83 | −1.89 | −0.42 | 0.684 |
| 20-day | 227 | −1.61% | −1.74% | −1.14% | 44% | 42% | **−3.30** | **−3.34** | −0.96 | 0.827 |
| 60-day | 225 | −4.39% | −4.56% | −3.32% | 33% | 37% | **−5.69** | **−5.41** | −1.38 | 0.891 |

Read it carefully. Against **zero**, the 20- and 60-day breakdown short returns
clear the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar (t = −3.30, −5.69) — but that is the **equity drift
premium working against every short position**, not the figure: a *random* day
shorted in the same stocks loses **−1.14% / −3.32%** over the same windows, close to
the breakdown's own **−1.61% / −4.39%**. The honest **Welch *t* of breakdown vs base
rate is only −0.42 to −1.38** — nowhere near 2, and *wrong-signed for the bearish
thesis at every horizon* (the confirmed breakdown short does **worse**, not better,
than a random short) — and the **date-shuffle placebo** says random shorts beat the
dome breakdown **68–89% of the time** (p = 0.684 / 0.827 / 0.891). The dome adds
**nothing** over just shorting a random day — if anything it is a mildly *worse* day
to pick.

## Robustness — no detector knob rescues it

Chart figures are subjective, so the fair worry is "you drew the dome wrong."
Varying the window length and the fit threshold leaves the verdict intact; the
breakdown-vs-base *t* never clears 2 in magnitude, and one configuration even flips
sign in the believer's favour without ever approaching significance.

| variation | n breakdowns | gross (20d, short) | one-sample *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `base_len` = 60 | 222 | −0.78% | −1.64 | **+0.75** | 0.197 |
| **`base_len` = 90** | **227** | **−1.61%** | **−3.30** | **−0.96** | **0.827** |
| `base_len` = 120 | 183 | −1.73% | −3.02 | −1.03 | 0.884 |
| `R²_min` = 0.45 | 295 | −1.40% | −3.18 | −0.59 | 0.748 |
| `R²_min` = 0.70 | 83 | −1.90% | −2.32 | −0.93 | 0.832 |

The breakdown-vs-base *t* ranges from **−1.03 to +0.75** across every configuration
— never significant, and at the shortest window (`base_len=60`) it actually points
in the *bullish* direction (a confirmed dome breakdown modestly *outperforming* a
random short — consistent with a short-term oversold bounce, though far from
certified itself).

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic panel we **plant the dome shape**. With `edge = 0` the shape is
present but there is **no** post-breakdown continuation — a true null the detector
must NOT turn into a decline edge. With `edge < 0` we plant a real decline the
detector must recover. Building this control surfaced a genuine methodological
pitfall — a naively-anchored planted dome can leak its own tail-end decline into the
"clean" forward window (documented in
[`rounding_top/data.py`](../rounding_top/data.py)) — fixed by anchoring the shape to
the exact bar the live detector references and widening the flat pad at the support
level so the sliding lookback window doesn't reference a still-elevated interior
dome level as "support" for many bars after the plant ends.

| planted edge | n breakdowns | gross (20d, short) | base rate (short) | one-sample *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* | win% |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (shape only, no continuation) | 145 | −0.20% | −0.40% | −0.44 | +0.42 | 0.351 | 53% |
| **−0.10** (real planted decline) | 143 | +3.18% | +0.15% | **+5.37** | **+5.11** | **0.000** | 71% |

With **no** continuation the control's breakdown-vs-base *t* sits at **+0.42**
(p = 0.351) — it does not fake a decline edge from a pretty shape. With a real
planted decline it jumps to **t = +5.11** (p = 0.000): the detector *can* find
continuation when it exists, so the real-tape null is a genuine null, not a blind
detector. **Checked across 20 seeds** (never a single lucky stream): null mean
Welch *t* = **−0.17** (sd 0.95), **|t| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** — essentially the
nominal false-positive rate of a well-calibrated test, not a systematic tell.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The confirmed dome breakdown's forward short return (**−1.61%
  at 20 days, −4.39% at 60**) **does not beat the every-bar SHORT base rate**
  (−1.14% / −3.32%): Welch *t* = −0.96 / −1.38, date-shuffle placebo *p* = 0.827 /
  0.891 — random shorts beat the pattern 83–89% of the time. The one-sample *t* vs
  zero (−3.30 / −5.69) is the **equity drift premium working against every short**,
  not a pattern signal. Survivorship here works *against* the bearish claim (the
  worst confirmed outcomes — delistings, bankruptcies — are structurally absent from
  a 2026-survivors panel) and there is still nothing to find.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no excess over a random short to harvest; 5 bps
  of cost plus a modest 30 bps/yr borrow rate turn an already-zero edge more
  negative still. Nothing to size, so capacity and impact are moot.
- **"Distribution signal"? — NOT SUPPORTED.** Across base-window {60, 90, 120} and
  fit R² {0.45, 0.55, 0.70} the breakdown-vs-base *t* **never clears 2 in magnitude**
  (range −1.03 to +0.75), and the shortest window even points the *wrong* way for
  the bearish thesis. A rounding top is an after-the-fact *description* of a top that
  already formed, not a forward edge — the mirror image of Study 416's rounding
  bottom, reaching the same conclusion from the other side of the tape.
